# Cast Iron Cookware Care

## Seasoning a Cast Iron Pan

Seasoning is the layer of polymerized oil baked into the porous iron surface that provides
non-stick properties and prevents rust. To season a new or stripped pan, wash with soap and
water, dry completely, then apply a thin layer of flaxseed oil, lard, or Crisco to all surfaces.
Wipe away excess oil until the pan looks almost dry. Bake upside down at 450 to 500 degrees
Fahrenheit for one hour. Let cool in the oven. Repeat three to six times for a durable base.

## Cooking with Cast Iron

Cast iron heats slowly but retains heat exceptionally well once hot. Preheat the pan gradually
over medium heat for five minutes before adding fat. The high heat retention makes cast iron
ideal for searing steaks, frying chicken, and baking cornbread. Avoid cooking acidic foods
like tomato sauce or citrus dishes for extended periods, as acid strips the seasoning.

## Cleaning and Maintenance

Clean the pan while still warm using a stiff brush or chain mail scrubber with hot water.
Avoid soaking in water or putting in the dishwasher, which causes rust. A small amount of
dish soap occasionally is acceptable on a well-seasoned pan. Dry the pan completely on the
stove over low heat. Apply a very thin layer of oil while still warm and wipe away the excess
before storing to maintain the seasoning.

## Restoring Rust

A rusty cast iron pan can be fully restored. Scrub with steel wool and dish soap to remove all
rust and old seasoning. Rinse and dry immediately. Re-season from scratch using the process above.
Cast iron is nearly indestructible and a well-maintained pan can last for generations.
